title: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
summary: Why search runs a cheap high-recall stage before costly rerankers: the recall ceiling, latency budgets per stage, bi-encoder vs late interaction vs cross-encoder, LLM listwise reranking and distillation.
outcomes: Explain why a reranker can never exceed the recall of the candidate list it receives, and choose candidate depth k
Compute the latency of a 3-stage cascade from per-stage depth and throughput and fit it to a budget
Compare bi-encoders, ColBERT late interaction and cross-encoders by when query and document meet, and compute MaxSim
Trace a sliding-window listwise LLM reranker and count its calls
Explain how distillation moves an expensive stage's quality into a cheaper one

lessons.title: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate

blocks.md:
The most accurate relevance models read the query and a document **together**. A cross-encoder such as monoBERT (Nogueira and Cho, 2019) feeds `[CLS] query [SEP] passage` through BERT and turns the `[CLS]` vector into a probability of relevance. Nothing can be precomputed, because every score depends on both texts.

Khattab and Zaharia measured what that costs: BERT-base reranking BM25's top 1000 MS MARCO passages took 10,700 ms per query on one Tesla V100 GPU. That is about 10.7 ms per passage.

blocks.prompt: MS MARCO has 8.8 million passages. At 10.7 ms per passage, how long would BERT-base need to score the whole collection for a single query?
blocks.reveal: 8.8 million x 10.7 ms = 94,160 seconds, about **26 hours per query**. Even a 100x faster GPU would leave you at roughly 16 minutes. Exhaustive scoring with the best model is not an engineering problem you can tune away; you need to score far fewer documents.

blocks.md: The way out is a **cascade** (also called multi-stage ranking or retrieve-then-rerank). Wang, Lin and Metzler (SIGIR 2011) describe it as a sequence of increasingly complex ranking functions that progressively prune documents and refine the order of the survivors. Early stages are cheap and see many documents; later stages are expensive and see few. They borrowed the intuition from Viola and Jones' face detector, which rejects easy negatives with simple classifiers before running costly ones.

blocks.caption: Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model: stage t costs its per-document unit cost U_t times the number of documents R_t it scores. Each stage passes a shorter list k_t to the next one.

blocks.title: A three-stage cascade: BM25, then monoBERT, then duoBERT

scenes.caption: Nogueira, Yang, Cho and Lin (2019) build this pipeline on MS MARCO. The corpus holds 8.8M passages; the query cannot afford a neural model on all of them.
Stage H0: BM25 over an inverted index returns k0 = 1000 candidates (Anserini: about 62 ms per query). Its job is recall: get the relevant passages somewhere into the list.
Stage H1: monoBERT scores each of the 1000 candidates independently (1000 inferences) and keeps the top k1 = 50.
Stage H2: duoBERT compares ordered pairs of the 50 survivors: 50 x 49 = 2450 inferences, more than monoBERT's 1000, but only on a list it could afford.
The final list goes to the user (or to an LLM in a RAG system). Every stage only reorders and truncates what it was given.

blocks.md: **monoBERT** is *pointwise*: it scores one (query, passage) pair at a time. **duoBERT** is *pairwise*: given (query, $d_i$, $d_j$) it estimates $p_{ij}$, the probability that $d_i$ is more relevant than $d_j$. Those pair scores are folded back into one score per passage, for example by summing:

blocks.caption: duoBERT's SUM aggregation. The paper also tested BINARY (count wins with p above 0.5), MIN, MAX and SAMPLE; MAX made results worse than monoBERT alone.

blocks.md: On MS MARCO dev, MRR@10 went from 18.7 (Anserini BM25) to 37.2 with monoBERT and 38.2 with monoBERT plus duoBERT-SUM; on the held-out evaluation set duoBERT added 0.5 points. The paper's point is not only the final number: because each stage controls how many candidates it admits, you can pick an operating point on the quality versus latency curve.

Each stage has a different job. The first stage must not lose relevant documents (recall); precision barely matters there, because later stages discard junk. The last stage must put the best documents on top (precision at the top) and only has to be good on a short list.
A reranker never finds anything. It can only reorder the list it receives. If stage 1 missed a document, no later stage, however large, can bring it back.

blocks.question: Why does the pipeline run duoBERT on monoBERT's top 50 instead of directly on BM25's top 1000?
options: duoBERT cannot read passages that BM25 retrieved
Pairwise scoring grows as k(k-1): 1000 candidates would need 999,000 inferences instead of 2450
duoBERT is less accurate than monoBERT, so it should see fewer documents
BM25 scores must be normalized before a pairwise model can use them
blocks.explain: Pairwise cost is quadratic in the list length. On 1000 candidates, duoBERT would need 1000 x 999 = 999,000 inferences per query, about 290 times the 3450 that monoBERT plus duoBERT on 50 use. Putting the quadratic model last, on a short list, is exactly the cascade idea.

blocks.question: Under Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model, you double k0 from 500 to 1000 in a BM25 plus monoBERT pipeline. What happens to monoBERT's cost per query?
options: It stays the same, because monoBERT runs once per query
It grows by about log 2
It roughly doubles, because cost is unit cost times the number of documents scored
It quadruples
blocks.explain: monoBERT scores each candidate independently, so its cost is U x k0. Nogueira et al. report exactly this: latency increases linearly with the number of candidates, while quality shows diminishing returns.

lessons.title: Candidate depth k and the recall ceiling

blocks.md: **Recall@k** is the fraction of a query's relevant documents that appear in the top $k$ of a ranked list. For a cascade, the recall@k of the list that stage 1 hands over (with $k = k_0$) is a hard ceiling on everything after it.

A toy query has **4 relevant documents**. The first stage ranks them at positions 2, 7, 19 and 140. Suppose the reranker is *perfect*: it always puts every relevant candidate it receives on top. How good can the final top 10 be?

blocks.title: Rerank depth k decides what the perfect reranker can see

scenes.caption: The first 20 positions of the stage 1 list. R marks a relevant document; the fourth relevant one sits at rank 140, off screen.
k = 5: only the document at rank 2 is passed on. Recall@5 = 1/4 = 0.25, so even a perfect reranker's top 10 holds 1 of 4 relevant documents.
k = 10: ranks 2 and 7 are in. Recall@10 = 0.5. The reranker can move both to the top, but cannot invent the other two.
k = 20: rank 19 joins. Recall@20 = 0.75, and the best possible final recall@10 is now 0.75.
k = 100 still gives 0.75: nothing new between 20 and 100. Any k of at least 140 reaches the last relevant document and recall 1.0; k = 200, for example, costs 10 times the reranking of k = 20.

blocks.caption: The ceiling. Rel is the set of relevant documents for the query and Top_k is what stage 1 passes on. Any metric that only rewards relevant documents (MRR, nDCG, recall) is capped the same way.

blocks.prompt: Khattab and Zaharia report two ColBERT setups on MS MARCO dev. One reranks the official BM25 top 1000; the other retrieves end to end with its own vector index. The model is the same. Which has higher MRR@10, and why?
blocks.reveal: End to end wins: **36.0** versus **34.8** MRR@10. Reranking BM25's list caps recall@1000 at 81.4%, the recall of the BM25 list itself. End-to-end ColBERT reaches 96.8% recall@1000, so it can surface relevant passages that BM25 never retrieved. Same scorer, higher ceiling.

blocks.title: Recall of different first stages on MS MARCO dev (%)

scenes.caption: Recall@50. A cheap first stage keeps only 59.2% of relevant passages in its top 50 (Anserini BM25). Document expansion (docTTTTTquery) and ColBERT do much better at the same depth.
Recall@200. Going 4x deeper buys BM25 another 14.6 points. End-to-end ColBERT is already at 92.3%.
Recall@1000. ColBERT reranking the official BM25 list is stuck at 81.4%, exactly that list's recall: the ceiling in action. End-to-end ColBERT reaches 96.8%.

blocks.md:
Deeper is better for recall, but not proportionally for quality. Nogueira et al. varied $k_0$ for monoBERT: compared with $k_0 = 1000$, they got more than half of the quality gain with about a fifth of the inferences. They also note that a deep list makes monoBERT score documents with quite low BM25 scores, which shows how weak BM25's own ordering is lower down.

The right $k$ is where stage 1's recall curve flattens, subject to the latency budget of the next stage (lesson 4).

Measure stage 1 on its own. Log recall@k for k in 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 on a labeled query set. If recall is low, upgrading the reranker is wasted money: improve the first stage (hybrid retrieval, document expansion, a better embedding model) or raise k.

blocks.question: Your RAG search uses BM25 top 100 and a strong cross-encoder. You swap in a cross-encoder twice as large and nDCG@10 barely moves. Stage 1 recall@100 is 0.62. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The new cross-encoder is undertrained
The ceiling: 38% of relevant documents never reach the reranker, so stage 1 recall or k must improve
nDCG@10 cannot measure reranker quality
k = 100 is too deep and confuses the reranker
blocks.explain: With recall@100 of 0.62, the reranker never sees 38% of relevant documents. Bigger rerankers only reorder the 62% they receive. Raise the ceiling: hybrid first stage, better embeddings, or a larger k if the budget allows.

blocks.question: In the toy above (relevant at ranks 2, 7, 19, 140), you rerank the top 20 with a perfect reranker. What is the final recall@10?
blocks.explain: Three relevant documents (ranks 2, 7, 19) are in the top 20; the perfect reranker moves all three into the top 10. The fourth, at rank 140, never arrives. 3/4 = 0.75.

lessons.title: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes

blocks.md:
Every neural scorer in a cascade is defined by **when query and document meet**:

- **Bi-encoder** (dense retrieval): encode query and document separately into one vector each and take a dot product. Document vectors are computed offline and indexed for nearest-neighbor search.
- **Cross-encoder**: concatenate query and document and run the full transformer on the pair. Every layer can compare every query token with every document token, but nothing can be precomputed.
- **Late interaction** (ColBERT): encode each side separately, but keep **one vector per token**, and compare them with a cheap operator at query time.

blocks.title: When do query and document meet?

scenes.caption: Bi-encoder: the document side runs offline. At query time you encode only the query, then one dot product per document, which an ANN index can search over millions of vectors.
Late interaction: still encoded separately (documents offline), but each side keeps a vector per token. The score sums, over query tokens, the best match among document tokens.
Cross-encoder: one transformer reads the pair together, so attention mixes query and document from the first layer. Most accurate, but a full forward pass per (query, document) at query time.

blocks.md: ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, SIGIR 2020) defines the late-interaction score as a sum of maximum similarities. Token vectors are L2-normalized, so each dot product is a cosine in $[-1, 1]$:

blocks.caption: For each query token, find its best-matching document token and add that similarity. Document tokens that match nothing contribute nothing.

scenes.caption: Cosines between 3 query tokens and the tokens of doc A (left 5 columns) and doc C (right 5). Vectors are hand-made 5-dimensional toys, not real ColBERT outputs.
Doc A: each query token has a near-perfect partner (reset with reboot 0.99, router 1.00, 651 1.00). MaxSim = 0.99 + 1.00 + 1.00 = 2.99. The off-topic warranty and refund tokens are simply ignored.
Doc C is vaguely about networking. Best matches are only 0.65 (help), 0.84 (modem) and 0.57 (issue): MaxSim = 2.06. Nothing in it mentions error 651.

Mean-pool each side into one vector instead (a crude bi-encoder) and the order flips: cosine 0.864 for C versus 0.711 for A, because A's average is dragged toward its shopping tokens. Per-token matching keeps the precise evidence.

blocks.md: The cost differences are large. Reranking the BM25 top 1000 on MS MARCO with one V100 (Khattab and Zaharia, Table 1):

blocks.title: Reranking BM25 top 1000 on MS MARCO: cost and quality

scenes.caption: Rerank latency per query in ms. ColBERT takes 61 ms, BERT-base 10,700 ms (over 170 times slower) and BERT-large 32,900 ms.
MRR@10 on dev (x 1000 to share the axis): 349, 360 and 365. ColBERT is within about 1 to 1.6 points of the cross-encoders at a tiny fraction of the cost.

blocks.md:
Where did ColBERT's 61 ms go? Only 13 ms was query encoding plus interaction; the rest was gathering the precomputed document vectors and moving them to the GPU. Late interaction shifts cost from compute to **storage and memory traffic**: the MS MARCO index with 128-dimensional vectors at 4 bytes per dimension took 286 GiB.

ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022) compresses each token vector as a centroid id plus a 1- or 2-bit-per-dimension residual: 20 or 36 bytes instead of 256 bytes at 16-bit precision, shrinking the index 6 to 10 times.

Cross-encoders come in other shapes too. **monoT5** (Nogueira, Jiang and Lin, 2020) feeds `Query: q Document: d Relevant:` to T5 and ranks by the softmax over just the logits of the tokens `true` and `false`. With BM25 top 1000 on MS MARCO dev it scored 0.383 MRR@10 (T5-large) against 0.372 for BERT-large, and it was much more data-efficient with few training examples.

Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

blocks.question: Which scorer could you put directly over a 50-million-document index as the **first** stage?
options: A cross-encoder, if you batch on a large GPU
A bi-encoder or late-interaction model, because document vectors are precomputed and searchable with ANN
Only BM25; neural models cannot be first stages
duoBERT with the SAMPLE aggregation
blocks.explain: First stages need precomputed document representations so the query can be matched with an index. Bi-encoders give one vector per document; ColBERT indexes token vectors and retrieves end to end. A cross-encoder has nothing to index: it needs a forward pass per pair.

blocks.question: In the MaxSim toy, you append five more unrelated tokens to doc A. What happens to A's MaxSim score?
options: It drops, because the average similarity falls
It rises, because more tokens means more matches
It is unchanged unless a new token beats an existing best match
It becomes undefined because A is longer than the query
blocks.explain: MaxSim takes, for each query token, the maximum over document tokens. Extra tokens can only raise a maximum, never lower it, and unrelated ones (low cosine) leave the maxima at 0.99, 1.00, 1.00. Mean pooling, in contrast, is diluted by them.

lessons.title: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines

blocks.md: A cascade is designed backwards from a **latency budget**: the time the product allows for one search, say 150 ms. Using the cost model from lesson 1, each stage costs roughly (candidates scored) x (time per candidate), and the stages run one after another, so their times add up.

We need per-document costs. The Sentence Transformers docs list throughput for their MS MARCO cross-encoders (the Hugging Face model cards say they were measured on a V100 GPU; treat them as relative):

- `ms-marco-MiniLM-L2-v2`: 4100 docs/s, NDCG@10 71.01 on TREC DL 19
- `ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2`: 1800 docs/s, NDCG@10 74.30
- `ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2`: 960 docs/s, NDCG@10 74.31

The 2-layer model is about 4.3 times faster than the 12-layer one and a few points worse: a natural cheap middle stage.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: stage 1 (hybrid retrieval) is assumed to take 20 ms; reranking time is candidates divided by throughput, ignoring batching overheads, network hops and tail effects. Here k_1 and k_2 are the lists entering stages 2 and 3 (lesson 1 called BM25's output k_0).

blocks.title: Accounting for a 3-stage cascade
blocks.code:
def search(query):
    spent = 0.0
    cands = hybrid_retrieve(query, k=200)   # stage 1
    spent += 20.0                           # assumed
    s = minilm_l2.predict([(query, d) for d in cands])
    cands = top(cands, s, k=30)             # stage 2
    spent += 1000 * 200 / 4100
    s = minilm_l12.predict([(query, d) for d in cands])
    final = top(cands, s, k=10)             # stage 3
    spent += 1000 * 30 / 960
    return final, spent

scenes.caption: Stage 1 returns k1 = 200 fused candidates. We assume it costs 20 ms.
Stage 2: the 2-layer cross-encoder scores all 200 at 4100 docs/s: 48.8 ms. It keeps the top 30.
Stage 3: the 12-layer cross-encoder scores only 30 at 960 docs/s: 31.3 ms. The final 10 are returned.
Total about 100 ms, inside a 150 ms budget. Running the 12-layer model on all 200 instead would cost 208.3 ms for that stage alone.

blocks.title: Single expensive stage versus a cascade (simplified model)

scenes.caption: One stage: the 12-layer model on all 200 candidates. 20 + 208.3 = 228.3 ms, far over the 150 ms budget (marker).
Cascade: L2 on 200 (48.8 ms), then L12 on 30 (31.3 ms). Done at 100.0 ms, with 50 ms of headroom.
Spend the headroom on recall: stage 1 passes 400 candidates. L2 now takes 97.6 ms and the total is 148.8 ms, just under budget. Deeper k1 raises the recall ceiling.

blocks.title: Total latency as the middle-stage depth k1 grows

scenes.caption: Defaults: t1 = 20 ms, k2 = 30. The cascade line crosses the 150 ms budget at k1 of about 405; the single 12-layer stage crosses it near k1 = 125.
Raise k2 to 80: the final stage costs 83.3 ms, and the largest affordable k1 falls to about 191. Every stage competes for the same budget.

blocks.md: Engines expose the cascade as configuration. **Vespa** has explicit phases: a `first-phase` expression runs on every retrieved hit on each content node, a `second-phase` expression reranks the best hits per node (100 by default; `total-rerank-count` caps the total across nodes), and a `global-phase` runs in the stateless container on the merged top hits (100 by default, set with `rerank-count` or the `ranking.globalPhase.rerankCount` query property). The docs name cross-encoders, run as ONNX models, as the typical global-phase use case.

scenes.caption: The stateless container scatters the query to every content node.
Each node retrieves matches (for example with weakAnd or nearest-neighbor operators) and scores all of them with the cheap first-phase expression.
Each node reranks its own best hits with the costlier second-phase expression, close to the data (for example a GBDT model).
Nodes return their best hits plus any match-features the global phase needs.
The container merges, then reranks the global top hits, for example with a cross-encoder in ONNX, possibly on a GPU.

blocks.md: **Elasticsearch** offers two forms. The `rescore` parameter reranks the top `window_size` hits **on each shard** (default 10) with a query, script or learning-to-rank model; several rescorers can run in sequence, and the docs suggest a larger window first and smaller windows for costlier later rescorers. The `text_similarity_reranker` retriever sends the top `rank_window_size` documents (default 10) of a child retriever to a rerank inference endpoint such as a cross-encoder:

blocks.caption: Rerank the top 100 BM25 hits with a cross-encoder endpoint. Without rank_window_size the reranker would only see 10 documents.

blocks.md: Defaults are shallow. Both Elasticsearch's rescore window_size and text_similarity_reranker's rank_window_size default to 10, so an unconfigured reranker can only shuffle the first page. Also keep the window fixed across pages: the docs warn that changing window_size while paginating can make top hits shift.

blocks.question: With t1 = 20 ms, k2 = 30 at 960 docs/s and the cheap reranker at 4100 docs/s, what is the largest k1 that fits a 150 ms budget in this model?
options: About 200
About 1000
About 125
About 400
blocks.explain: The precise stage costs 1000 x 30 / 960 = 31.25 ms. That leaves 150 - 20 - 31.25 = 98.75 ms for the cheap stage, which scores 4.1 docs per ms: 98.75 x 4.1 = 404.9 candidates.

blocks.question: Users report that a relevant document at BM25 rank 15 never moves up, even though the cross-encoder scores it highest when tested alone. The pipeline uses text_similarity_reranker with no extra settings. What is wrong?
options: The cross-encoder needs min_score set to 0
rank_window_size defaults to 10, so the document at rank 15 is never sent to the reranker
BM25 scores override reranker scores
The reranker only works with kNN child retrievers
blocks.explain: The reranker only sees the child retriever's top rank_window_size documents, 10 by default. Rank 15 sits outside the window, so this is the recall ceiling again, created by configuration. Set rank_window_size to the depth your budget allows.

lessons.title: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages

blocks.md: monoBERT scores one document at a time (**pointwise**) and duoBERT compares two (**pairwise**). A **listwise** reranker looks at several candidates at once and outputs their order. RankGPT (Sun et al., EMNLP 2023) does this with an instruction-following LLM: passages are given identifiers `[1]`, `[2]`, ... and the model is asked to output a permutation such as `[2] > [3] > [1]`, with no scores at all.

An LLM cannot read 100 passages in one prompt comfortably, so RankGPT uses a **sliding window** with window size $w$ and step $s$, moving from the **back** of the list to the front. It first reorders positions $M-w+1$ to $M$, then slides up by $s$ and reorders again, until it reaches the top. The paper's experiments rerank BM25's top 100 with $w = 20$, $s = 10$.

blocks.title: One back-to-front pass: 8 passages, w = 4, s = 2

scenes.caption: Stage 1 order. Grades (0 to 3) are hidden from the model; we show them to follow the pass. The best passage, h (grade 3), sits last. Simplified: the LLM is assumed to sort each window perfectly.
Window 1 covers positions 5 to 8. The LLM sorts it: h jumps from 8 to 5.
Window 2 covers positions 3 to 6 (slid up by s = 2). h is carried along because windows overlap by w - s = 2, and climbs to 3.

Window 3 covers positions 1 to 4. h reaches the top and c (grade 2) is second: the top w - s = 2 are exactly right. But b (grade 0) at 4 still sits above e (grade 1): lower positions are only partly sorted.

blocks.caption: With M = 100, w = 20, s = 10, one pass makes 9 LLM calls and the model reads 9 x 20 = 180 passages, nearly twice the list, because windows overlap.

blocks.prompt: Assume the LLM sorts every window perfectly. After one back-to-front pass with w = 20 and s = 10, which part of the final list is guaranteed to be in the correct order?
blocks.reveal: Exactly the **top w - s = 10**. Each window hands its best w - s documents to the next window, so any document that belongs in the global top 10 is never left behind. Our simulation over 20,000 random lists with varied w and s found no exception. Below position 10 there is no guarantee, as b above e showed. That matches what you want from a final stage: a correct top, cheap tail.

blocks.md: The paper's ablations show the cascade logic inside the LLM stage. Results were highly sensitive to the initial order: starting from a random or reversed BM25 list hurt, because one pass relies on a decent starting order. Extra passes could raise nDCG@10 but lowered nDCG@1. On BEIR, letting GPT-4 rerank only the top 30 of ChatGPT's output gave good results at about a fifth of the cost of GPT-4 alone. The authors also flag cost, latency and unstable generation as obstacles to deploying LLM rerankers directly.

**Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

Three distillation recipes, each moving quality one stage earlier:

- **RankGPT permutation distillation**: ChatGPT ranks 20 BM25 candidates for 10,000 MS MARCO queries; a cross-encoder student is trained with RankNet on the 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 ordered pairs per query. A roughly 440M-parameter DeBERTa student beat the 3B monoT5 by 1.67 nDCG on average on BEIR.
- **Margin-MSE** (Hofstätter et al., 2020): cross-encoder (BERT-CAT) teachers train ColBERT, a BERT dot-product bi-encoder and others to match the teacher's score *margin* between a relevant and a non-relevant passage.
- **ColBERTv2**: a 22M-parameter MiniLM cross-encoder scores retrieved passages, and ColBERT is trained with a KL-divergence loss toward those scores over 64 passages per example.

blocks.caption: Margin-MSE. M_s is the student, M_t the teacher. Matching margins instead of raw scores lets each architecture keep its own natural score range; Hofstätter et al. observed that different architectures settle into very different ranges.
RankNet loss used for RankGPT's permutation distillation: r_i is the teacher's rank of passage i and s_i the student's score. Every pair the teacher ordered becomes a training signal.

blocks.md: A practical modern cascade: hybrid first stage (BM25 plus a distilled bi-encoder) with k in the hundreds, a small distilled cross-encoder on that list, and optionally an LLM listwise reranker on only the top 20 or 30. Log candidates and scores per stage so you can measure each stage's recall and gain separately.

blocks.question: RankGPT reranks M = 100 passages with w = 20 and s = 10. You switch to w = 20, s = 5 to give passages more chances to move. How many LLM calls does one pass now make?
blocks.explain: ceil((100 - 20) / 5) + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17 calls, reading 17 x 20 = 340 passages. Smaller steps mean more overlap and almost double the cost of s = 10. The guaranteed-correct top also grows, from w - s = 10 to 15.

blocks.question: Why does Margin-MSE train the student on score margins instead of making it reproduce the teacher's raw scores?
options: Different architectures naturally produce scores on different scales; only the ordering matters, and the margin preserves it
Raw scores are not available from cross-encoders
Margins are cheaper to compute at query time
MSE cannot be applied to raw scores
blocks.explain: A dot-product bi-encoder or ColBERT produces scores on a very different scale from a cross-encoder. Forcing the same raw values fights the architecture. Ranking only needs the student to separate relevant from non-relevant by the same amount, which is what the margin captures.

blocks.question: Your LLM listwise reranker on the top 100 meets quality targets but costs too much per query. Which change follows the cascade principle best?
options: Run the LLM on the top 100 but with a random initial order to avoid bias
Drop stage 1 and let the LLM read the whole corpus in windows
Let a distilled cross-encoder rerank the 100 and send only its top 20 to the LLM in one window
Increase the step size to 20 so windows no longer overlap
blocks.explain: Put the cheap model where the list is long and the expensive model where it is short: one LLM window instead of 9 calls. RankGPT's own GPT-4-on-top-30 result follows the same pattern. Random initial order hurt in the paper, and s = w removes the overlap that carries good passages forward.
